\maketitle

\section{Purpose}

This note fixes terminology for a recurring failure mode in the formalization
of the low individual degree test paper, \path{arXiv:2009.12982}.  It
complements the note-writing policy in \path{docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex} and
the source-statement audit tracked historically in \ghissue{1458}.  The current
source-boundary proof holes are tracked in \ghissue{1507} and \ghissue{422}.
A proof may be blocked at
an intermediate mathematical assertion.  If that assertion is added as a new
hypothesis to a theorem labelled as a paper theorem, the resulting \Lean{}
theorem
may be correct as a conditional statement, but it is no longer the theorem in
the cited source.  The apparent proof has not closed the paper theorem; it has
moved a proof obligation into the theorem statement.

The protocol below distinguishes such proof debt from legitimate formal
boundary conditions and from genuine mathematical corrections.  It is meant for
contributors and reviewers who must decide whether a bridge, residual, repair,
input, or obligation structure is a proved local construction, a tracked proof
gap, or statement drift which must be repaired before a theorem may be
advertised as a source theorem.  The default rule is restrictive: such data
must not be added to a paper-facing theorem unless it is part of the cited
source statement or a documented faithful encoding of its ambient hypotheses.

\section{Basic objects}

\paragraph{Source theorem.}
A source theorem is a theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary in the paper
source under \path{references/ldt-paper/}.  Its hypotheses and conclusion are
the mathematical ground truth, subject only to faithful formal encoding and to
documented paper-gap corrections.

\paragraph{Paper-facing declaration.}
A \Lean{} declaration is paper-facing when it is named or cited as the
formalization of a source theorem, for instance through a blueprint
\verb|\lean{}| link on a theorem environment carrying a paper label.  Such a
declaration must match the source theorem in its public statement.  In
particular, it may not add an unproved bridge, residual, repair, input,
obligation structure, or other proof-obligation hypothesis which the paper does
not assume.

\paragraph{Proof obligation.}
A proof obligation is an intermediate assertion needed by the proof of a source
theorem.  It may be a construction, an estimate, a transport lemma, or a
comparison between two formal representations.  If the paper proves or invokes
this assertion, then the formalization should state it as a separate lemma or
theorem and prove it from the upstream hypotheses.

\paragraph{Obligation discharger.}
An obligation discharger is a theorem or definition which constructs a proof
obligation from the paper hypotheses already available at that point in the
argument.  This is the preferred representation of missing work.  If the proof
is not yet complete, the discharger may temporarily contain a tracked
\verb|sorry|, but the paper-facing theorem should call it rather than assume
its output as an additional theorem hypothesis.

\paragraph{Conditional helper.}
A conditional helper is a separately named theorem whose statement explicitly
assumes a proof obligation.  Names such as
\leanid{mainFormal\_ofInternalObligations},
\leanid{orthonormalization\_ofInput}, or names whose suffix advertises the
assumed obligation are permitted only when the declaration is not presented as
the source theorem.  A conditional helper is a quarantine for downstream proof
content; it does not close the source theorem.

\section{Bridge, residual, repair, input, and obligation structures}

The words \emph{bridge}, \emph{residual}, \emph{repair}, \emph{input}, and
\emph{obligation structure} name possible formal shapes.  They become dangerous
when their mathematical status is unclear or when their names make unproved
data look like acceptable hypotheses of a source theorem.

\paragraph{Bridge.}
A bridge should be a transport theorem between two already defined
mathematical forms: for example, a tensor-placement identity, a conversion
between two equivalent consistency relations, or a statement translating a
source object into a formal representation.  A bridge is harmless only after it
is proved from previously available assumptions.  It becomes proof debt when it
is assumed because the transport has not yet been proved.  It becomes theorem
drift when the assumed bridge is added to a paper-facing theorem.

\paragraph{Residual.}
A residual is a named remainder after part of an argument has been performed.
It is often a useful way to record the exact missing target after a completed
construction.  A residual may appear as the conclusion of a helper theorem or
as the input of a quarantined conditional helper.  It is not a permissible new
assumption on a paper theorem unless the paper itself assumes that residual.

\paragraph{Input.}
An input is a named bundle of data or hypotheses consumed by a construction or
conditional helper.  It is harmless only when each load-bearing field is either
part of the source hypotheses or is produced by an earlier theorem.  It becomes
proof debt when the bundle is merely assumed because the construction of its
fields is missing.  It becomes theorem drift when such a bundle is added to the
public statement of a source theorem.

\paragraph{Repair.}
A repair is a mathematical construction which replaces an approximate or
partial object by a better object, usually with a quantitative estimate.  In
the low individual degree test formalization, projectivization and
orthonormalization repairs are genuine mathematical operations.  A repair
should therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the
corresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead
of constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.

\paragraph{Obligation structure.}
An obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates
needed by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target
or as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement
drift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed
inside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is
proved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing
obligation.

\section{The main failure mode}

Suppose the paper proves
\[
  H \Longrightarrow C.
\]
During formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \(B\).  The
paper theorem should be represented as
\[
  H \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C
  \quad\text{inside the proof,}
\]
where \(B\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \(H\).  The following
public statement is a different theorem:
\[
  H \land B \Longrightarrow C.
\]
It is not unsound in \Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the
conclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a
conditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's
conclusion.

This is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge
hypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted
from the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide
the hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a
paper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a
named internal proof obligation.

\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}

Not every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are
faithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include
nonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a
quantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,
or decidability instances required by \Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable
when they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a
condition used implicitly in the paper.

The distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the
domain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a
mathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis
leaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the
hypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.

\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}

Definition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a
definition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,
then every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile
while proving statements about the wrong object.  Downstream theorem statements
can then be repaired piecemeal, but the development remains unstable because
the wrong definition is still upstream.

When a definition mismatch is found, the repair should proceed by a subtree
protocol.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Identify the source object and the formal object precisely.
  \item Freeze a source-faithful definition or state an adapter theorem
  relating the existing definition to the source object.
  \item Recheck the downstream theorem chain against that definition or adapter.
  \item Re-formalize the affected subtree from the corrected interface, rather
  than adding local hypotheses to each downstream theorem.
  \item If a downstream proof cannot be completed, record the missing obligation
  at the lowest point where the paper proof needs it.
\end{enumerate}

This is slower than editing a final theorem signature, but it prevents a local
definition error from becoming a global theorem-statement error.

\section{Allowed shapes}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.24\linewidth}p{0.31\linewidth}p{0.32\linewidth}}
\textbf{Shape} & \textbf{Allowed use} & \textbf{Forbidden use} \\
\hline
Paper-facing theorem & Matches the source statement up to faithful encoding &
Carries non-paper bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, or
proof-obligation hypotheses \\
Source-shaped theorem with a tracked \verb|sorry| & Default repair when the
source proof is blocked but the statement is known & Replaced by a strengthened
theorem statement merely to keep the file compiling \\
Conditional helper & Temporary quarantine for substantial proof content whose
remaining named obligation has not yet been discharged & Introduced merely to
avoid a \verb|sorry|, or linked as the source theorem or marked as
proof-complete for that theorem \\
Obligation discharger theorem & Constructs the obligation from paper hypotheses &
Merely restates the obligation as an assumption \\
Input bundle & Collects produced data for a local construction & Is assumed by a
source theorem instead of being produced \\
Obligation structure & Bundles constructed data and estimates & Hides unproved
fields that are then assumed by a source theorem \\
Paper-gap note & Documents a real mathematical or formal-statement divergence &
Justifies silent statement drift without a repair plan
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\section{Protocol for a blocked proof}

When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Read the cited source statement and the proof passage in
  \path{references/ldt-paper/}.
  \item Write the paper theorem form, the current \Lean{} theorem form, and the
  first missing intermediate assertion.
  \item Decide whether the missing assertion is a faithful boundary condition,
  a representation adapter, an ordinary lemma from the paper proof, or a real
  paper-gap discrepancy.
  \item If it is an ordinary lemma or adapter, create a named theorem which
  discharges that obligation.  Do not add it to the source theorem as a new
  hypothesis.
  \item Keep the source-labelled theorem itself in the source form, even if its
  proof must contain a tracked \verb|sorry|.  This is the default repair when
  the missing assertion has not yet been proved.
  \item Create a conditional helper only to quarantine substantial proof content
  that already exists and would otherwise be lost.  Do not create such a helper
  merely to avoid a \verb|sorry| or to keep making progress.  If a conditional
  helper remains, give it a conditional name, keep it separate from the
  paper-facing theorem, and record the obligation discharger that must eliminate
  it.
  \item If the source and formal statements genuinely differ, write or update a
  note under \path{docs/paper-gaps/} before marking the statement as aligned.
  \item Update the blueprint so that paper labels point only to paper-facing
  declarations.  Conditional helpers belong in remarks or implementation
  notes, not in the source theorem block.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Retirement criterion}

An auxiliary declaration should be removed from the main blueprint route, or
renamed and documented as a purely internal lemma, when all three of the
following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item it is not a statement in the cited paper and is not an explicitly cited
        outside result;
  \item no current proof of a paper-level target needs it as stated;
  \item it assumes stronger proof data, finite-length data, completion data,
        repair data, synchronization data, or package fields than the paper
        proof requires.
\end{enumerate}
If such a declaration is still useful as a formal intermediate result, it
should remain a lemma or a visibly conditional helper with a planned discharge.
It should not be a headline replacement for the paper theorem, and it should
not support a source-labelled blueprint \verb|\leanok| claim.

\section{Review questions}

A reviewer should first compare every paper-labelled declaration with the cited
source statement, checking both hypotheses and conclusion up to faithful formal
encoding.  Bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, and
proof-obligation assumptions should be absent from paper-facing theorem
signatures unless they occur in the paper.  If a conditional helper remains,
its name should be explicitly conditional and it should not support a source
theorem \verb|\leanok| claim.
Each load-bearing obligation-structure or input field should have a theorem
discharging it, a tracked issue, or an explicit \verb|sorry| at the obligation
site.  When a definition has changed, the downstream subtree should be checked
against the corrected definition rather than patched locally.  Finally, if the
formal statement genuinely differs from the source statement, a paper-gap note
should explain the mathematical difference and give a plan to remove or justify
it.

\section{Conclusion}

The project should prefer visible proof obligations over invisible statement
drift.  A tracked \verb|sorry| in the source-shaped theorem, or in the lowest
named internal obligation needed by its proof, is less misleading than a source
theorem whose assumptions have been strengthened.  Conditional helpers are not a
normal substitute for unfinished proofs; they are temporary quarantines for
substantial proof content, and they must remain conditional until the missing
obligation is discharged.  The paper-facing declaration is reserved for the
theorem proved by the paper, or for a documented corrected version whose
mathematical difference is explicit.

    10	\title{Documenting Possible Gaps, Counterexamples, and Formalization Deviations}
    11	\author{}
    12	\date{2026-04-29}
    13	
    14	\begin{document}
    15	\maketitle
    16	
    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.
   221	
   222	Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
   223	substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
   224	a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
   225	proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
   226	logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.
   227	
   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.
   241	
   242	Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
   243	\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
   244	\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
   245	the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
   246	equations.
   247	
   248	Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
   249	\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
   250	\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
   251	whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
   252	and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.
   253	
   254	The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
   255	there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
   256	in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
   257	be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
   258	footnotes.
   259	
   260	The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,
   261	that the matter is only notational, that an intermediate estimate needs a
   262	harmless correction, that a hypothesis is missing, that there is a theorem-level
   263	gap, or that the question remains open.  The classification should reflect the
   264	mathematics, not the amount of formal work required.
   265	
   266	\section{Decision Principle}
   267	
   268	The formal development should not silently replace the cited assertion by a
   269	different one.  If the formal statement differs from the cited source, the
   270	reason for the difference should be written down.  Conversely, the note should
   271	not overstate the conclusion.  A wrong intermediate scalar is not a fatal gap in
   272	the theorem if the corrected scalar is bounded by the error parameter appearing
   273	in the theorem statement.
   274	
   275	\end{document}

    21	\section{At a glance}
    22	
    23	\begin{itemize}
    24	  \item \textbf{Difficulty: easy.}  No step of the retained proof route is
    25	  in doubt.  The obstruction is that the error function claimed in the
    26	  statement of the combined-lines lemma of the Pauli basis analysis,
    27	  $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, is not delivered by either of the two
    28	  derivations printed in its source proof: one route establishes
    29	  $m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$, the other would give
    30	  $m^2 \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ and rests in addition on a distributional
    31	  decomposition that the stated sub-line lemma does not supply.  The
    32	  substance is deciding which error form the statement should carry and
    33	  confirming that the sole consumer tolerates it.
    34	  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs:} the
    35	  Cauchy--Schwarz inequality for state-dependent operator distances
    36	  (project-local, blueprint Chapter 12), mixture decompositions of
    37	  question distributions, and elementary averaging over restricted
    38	  line distributions; no new Mathlib surface beyond finite
    39	  expectations and inner-product estimates already used by the
    40	  low individual degree development.
    41	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight:} a \textbf{statement-level error-form
    42	  decision} plus about \textbf{one lemma interface} of checking that the
    43	  consumer absorbs an $m$ prefactor into its constants; the three chained
    44	  claims behind the retained route are ordinary Cauchy--Schwarz estimates,
    45	  on the order of \textbf{a few hundred lines} of formal proof in total
    46	  when that part of the development is reached.
    47	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split:} essentially \textbf{100\%
    48	  project-local}.  The estimates use only the project's state-dependent
    49	  distance calculus, the sub-line distribution, and elementary
    50	  probability on finite sets.
    51	  \item \textbf{Key inputs:} the combined point and line measurements and
    52	  the sub-line distribution of the Pauli basis analysis in
    53	  \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, and the error function of the classical soundness
    54	  theorem imported from \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}, into which the
    55	  corrected error form must be absorbed.  Tracked in \localissue{0002}.
    56	\end{itemize}
    57	
    58	\section{Key theorem forms}
    59	
    60	Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple of the Pauli basis
    61	test, $\ket{\hat\psi}$ is the expanded state of the projective strategy
    62	under analysis, succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, and all
    63	approximations are with respect to $\ket{\hat\psi}$.  For lines
    64	$\ell_X, \ell_Z$ in $\F_q^m$, the POVM $\{T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\}$,
    65	with outcomes pairs of polynomials of degree at most $md$ on the two
    66	lines, is the two-basis combined line measurement, and
    67	$\{\hat Q^{x,z}_{a,b}\}$ is the combined point measurement; their
    68	consistency errors are $\delta_P = \poly(\eps, md/q)$ and
    69	$\delta_Q = \poly(\eps)$ respectively, and
    70	$\delta_{\mathrm{Line}} = \poly(\eps)$ is the line--point consistency
    71	error of the strategy.  The lemma under discussion asserts that a
    72	measurement $\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, built for each line $\ell$ in
    73	$\F_q^{2m+2}$, is $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$-consistent, on average over
    74	the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$, with the combined point
    75	measurement on the extended coordinates, together with the
    76	register-swapped counterpart.%
    77	\footnote{In the mirror of the source consulted here,
    78	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}: the
    79	lemma statement, with the error form $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, is at
    80	lines~1020--1034 (label \path{lem:qld-4-13}); the central display with
    81	the first-route bound at lines~1134--1137
    82	(label \path{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency}); the three claims at
    83	lines~1140--1239 (labels \path{claim:17-1}--\path{claim:17-3}); the
    84	second-route conclusion $O(m^2\delta_P)$ at lines~1241--1245, preceded by
    85	a duplicated sentence whose second copy carries a malformed reference;
    86	the product-distribution estimate invoked there at lines~1055--1061
    87	(label \path{eq:qld-xz-lines-restricted}); and the sub-line lemma at
    88	lines~1063--1116 (label \path{lem:qld-sublines}).}
    89	The comparison involves four forms of the error function
    90	$\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}(\eps,m,d,q)$.
    91	\begin{enumerate}
    92	  \item \textbf{Source form.}
    93	  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = \poly(m^2\eps,\, md/q)$.  This is the form
    94	  printed in the statement.  Neither printed derivation supports it.
    95	  \item \textbf{Established form (first route).}
    96	  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}
    97	  = O\big(m\,(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4}
    98	  + \delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2})\big)$, a function of the form
    99	  $m \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)$.
   100	  \item \textbf{Second-route form (conditional).}
   101	  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = O(m^2 \delta_P)
   102	  = m^2 \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)$, conditional on a joint-law
   103	  decomposition that the sub-line lemma, as stated, does not provide.
   104	  \item \textbf{Consumer requirement.}  The unique consumer, the
   105	  polynomial-pair lemma, feeds $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$ into an error
   106	  of the form
   107	  $a(md)^a(\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ imported
   108	  from \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}; any bound
   109	  $m^{O(1)} \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ is absorbed by enlarging $a$ and

   113	\section{The source assertion and the two routes}
   114	
   115	The source proof in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar} constructs $\hat Q^{\ell}_f$ by
   116	averaging, over a distribution $D$ on tuples $(\ell, \ell_X, \ell_Z)$
   117	provided by its sub-line lemma, the pushforward of
   118	$T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}$ along a combining map, and reduces the lemma to a
   119	bound on the scalar consistency defect
   120	\begin{equation}
   121	  \Lambda \,=\,
   122	  \E_{(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z) \sim D}\
   123	  \E_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta) \in \ell}
   124	  \sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
   125	  \big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
   126	  \big(\Id - \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
   127	  \ket{\hat\psi}\,,
   128	  \tag{\path{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency}}
   129	\end{equation}
   130	in which the point $(x,z,\alpha,\beta)$ is uniform on $\ell$ and the sum
   131	ranges over pairs of line polynomials.  The proof then bounds $\Lambda$
   132	twice, by different routes and with different results, and the printed
   133	record is internally inconsistent: the display introducing $\Lambda$
   134	asserts the first-route bound, while the closing lines assert the
   135	second-route bound as the operative one; the lemma statement claims a
   136	third form matching neither.
   137	
   138	\paragraph{The first route.}
   139	Three claims are chained.  The combined point measurement
   140	$\hat Q^{x,z}$ is replaced by the ordered product of the two point
   141	measurements at cost $\delta_Q^{1/2}$; the $X$-point factor is removed at
   142	cost $m\,\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}$; and the remaining $Z$-point
   143	correlation is shown to be within
   144	$\sqrt{m}\,(\delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4} + \eps^{1/4})$ of one.  The
   145	factors of $m$ enter through the mixture structure of the sub-line
   146	distribution: each restricted line distribution carries mixture weight
   147	$1/(2m)$ in the line-point distribution, so an average bounded by
   148	$\delta$ over the full distribution is bounded only by $2m\delta$ over a
   149	restricted component and by $4m^2\delta$ over a product of two
   150	components, and the Cauchy--Schwarz steps halve the exponents.  Chaining
   151	the claims gives
   152	\begin{equation*}
   153	  \Lambda \,=\, O\big(m\,(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4}
   154	  + \delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2})\big)
   155	  \,=\, m \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)\,.
   156	\end{equation*}
   157	One intermediate assertion needs a harmless correction: the final line
   158	of the proof of the second claim asserts the bound
   159	$O(m^2 \delta_{\mathrm{Line}})$ for a consistency term that is close to
   160	one, rather than for its deficit.  Read as a bound on the deficit ---
   161	which is what the surrounding Cauchy--Schwarz argument requires and what
   162	the invoked line--point consistency provides after the mixture
   163	inflation --- the claim and its use are correct, with the square root of
   164	the deficit giving the stated cost $m\,\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}$.
   165	
   166	\paragraph{The second route.}
   167	After the chain, the source restarts: it asserts that, by Property~2 of
   168	its sub-line lemma, $\Lambda$ is a mixture, over types
   169	$\mathrm{v}_1, \mathrm{v}_2 \in \{\mathrm{ALine}, \mathrm{DLine}\}$ and
   170	indices $i, j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, of terms
   171	\begin{equation*}
   172	  \E_{(\ell_X, x) \sim D_{\mathrm{v}_1,i}}\
   173	  \E_{(\ell_Z, z) \sim D_{\mathrm{v}_2,j}}
   174	  \sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
   175	  \big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
   176	  \big(\Id - \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
   177	  \ket{\hat\psi}
   178	\end{equation*}
   179	over two \emph{independently} sampled restricted line-point pairs,
   180	bounds each term by $O(m^2\delta_P)$ using the restricted-distribution
   181	consequence of the two-basis line lemma, and concludes
   182	$\Lambda = O(m^2\delta_P)$.  The invoked decomposition concerns the
   183	\emph{joint} law of the pair $((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z))$, where $x$ and
   184	$z$ are the two blocks of the single point sampled on $\ell$.  Property~2
   185	of the sub-line lemma does not assert this joint law: it asserts the
   186	component-wise product law of the pair of \emph{lines}
   187	$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$, and the conditional uniformity of each point on its
   188	line separately --- equivalently, the laws of the two pairs
   189	$((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z'))$ and $((\ell_X, x'), (\ell_Z, z))$ in which
   190	the \emph{other} point is resampled independently.  These marginal
   191	statements are exactly what the first route's claims consume, each
   192	involving one point at a time; the joint decomposition used by the
   193	second route is a strictly stronger property and is not established by
   194	the lemma it is attributed to.

   196	\section{Why neither route yields the stated form}
   197	
   198	The stated error form is $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, a function of the two
   199	quantities $m^2\eps$ and $md/q$ that vanishes as both vanish.  The
   200	first-route bound is not dominated by any such function: along the
   201	scaling $\eps = m^{-4}$ with $q/(md) \to \infty$, both $m^2\eps = m^{-2}$
   202	and $md/q$ tend to $0$, while the term $m\,\eps^{1/4} = 1$ does not.
   203	Hence the established derivation supports no bound of the claimed form.
   204	The second-route bound, even granting the missing decomposition, carries
   205	the separate prefactor $m^2$: writing $\delta_P = \poly(\eps, md/q)$
   206	with some fixed positive exponents, the contribution
   207	$m^2 (md/q)^{c}$ is not dominated by any vanishing function of $m^2\eps$
   208	and $md/q$, as the scaling $\eps = 0$, $md/q = m^{-2/c}$ shows, and the
   209	$\eps$-contribution fails similarly for sublinear exponents.  Neither
   210	observation asserts that the \emph{conclusion} of the lemma is false for
   211	some error function of the claimed form; the defect is that the printed
   212	proof does not deliver it.
   213	
   214	For orientation, the algebraic identity
   215	$m\,\eps^{1/2} = (m^2\eps)^{1/2}$ shows what a derivation of the claimed
   216	$\eps$-dependence would need: a chain that loses only square roots in the
   217	$\eps$-type quantities \emph{after} the restricted-distribution
   218	inflation would produce terms of the shape $(m^2\eps)^{1/2}$.  The
   219	printed chain loses fourth roots, through two nested Cauchy--Schwarz
   220	steps applied to already square-rooted quantities, and its
   221	$md/q$-dependence enters as $m\,\delta_P^{1/4}$, which the claimed form
   222	cannot absorb.

   295	\section{Conclusion}
   296	
   297	There is a proof-level gap in the cited lemma, together with an
   298	intermediate inconsistency: the printed proof asserts two different
   299	bounds for the same consistency defect, the first-route bound
   300	$O(m(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4} +
   301	\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}))$ and the second-route bound
   302	$O(m^2\delta_P)$, the second resting on a joint-law decomposition that
   303	the sub-line lemma as stated does not supply; and the error form claimed
   304	in the lemma statement, $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, follows from neither.
   305	The first route is sound after a harmless deficit correction in its
   306	second claim and establishes $m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$.  The
   307	discrepancy is harmless downstream, since the sole consumer absorbs
   308	polynomial-in-$m$ prefactors into its constants.  The recommended
   309	resolution is to treat the corrected error form as operative while the
   310	source-labelled statement retains its printed form with the missing step
   311	explicitly tracked; strengthening the sub-line lemma to license the
   312	second route is optional, and no route to the claimed form is currently
   313	known.  We do not assert that the claimed form is false.

    61	Throughout, $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size, the tuple
    62	$(q,m,d)$ is admissible when moreover $d \ge 1$ and $m \mid q$, and

    64	over $\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$.  The comparison involves four

    67	  \item \textbf{Source theorem form} (the polynomial-pair measurement).  There

    69	  for universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, such that for every
    70	  admissible $(q,m,d)$ and every projective strategy for the Pauli basis test

   108	\section{The source assertion and the obstruction}
   109	
   110	We examine the final step of the subsection ``Applying the classical
   111	low-degree test'' in the analysis of the Pauli basis test in the compression
   112	paper of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen (MIP$^{*}$=RE,
   113	arXiv:2001.04383), whose quantum soundness component builds on the low
   114	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.%
   115	\footnote{Tracked in \localissue{0002}.  In the mirror of the source
   116	consulted here, the polynomial-pair lemma and its proof are at
   117	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
   118	lines~1267--1288; the sub-line lemma is at lines~1063--1116 and the combined
   119	line lemma at lines~1020--1034 of the same file.  The game parametrization
   120	with its divisibility, the index function, the soundness statement with its
   121	proof, and admissibility are at
   122	\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
   123	lines~33--35, 214--219, 413--458, and 958--961.}
   124	There, the combined point measurements
   125	$\{\hat Q^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_c\}$ and combined line measurements
   126	$\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, indexed by points of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and lines in
   127	$\F_q^{2m+2}$, are asserted to form a strategy for the classical low
   128	individual degree game with parameters
   129	\[
   130	  \mathsf{ldparams} = (q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)
   131	  \tag{\path{lem:qld-4-7}}
   132	\]
   133	of value $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$, and the quantum soundness theorem
   134	for that game is applied to produce the global polynomial-pair measurement.
   135	The two lemmas feeding this step are stated for the line-point distribution
   136	over $\F_q^{2m+2}$.
   137	
   138	The game, however, is parametrized by tuples $(q,m',d,k)$ with $q$ an
   139	admissible field size \emph{and $m'$ dividing $q$}.  The divisibility is not
   140	incidental: the question distribution is a conditionally linear distribution
   141	in which a uniform seed coordinate $s \in \F_q$, read as an integer in
   142	$\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, determines the axis or diagonal index through the unique
   143	$\chi(s)$ with
   144	\[
   145	  s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m'} + r, \qquad 0 \le r < \frac{q}{m'},
   146	  \tag{\path{eq:chi-func}}
   147	\]
   148	so that the $m'$ classes $\chi^{-1}(i)$ partition $\F_q$ into sets of equal
   149	size $q/m'$ and the index is uniform.  For $m' \nmid q$ neither the index
   150	function nor the line-point distribution built from it is defined.
   151	
   152	Admissibility of $(q,m,d)$ supplies only $m \mid q$.  Since an admissible $q$
   153	is a power of two, $m \mid q$ forces $m = 2^j$.  For $j \ge 1$ the integer
   154	$m+1 \ge 3$ is odd, so $2m+2 = 2(m+1)$ has an odd factor exceeding $1$ and
   155	divides no power of two; for $m = 1$ the condition $4 \mid q$ holds for every
   156	admissible $q$ except $q = 2$.  Thus the instantiation at dimension $2m+2$ is
   157	undefined for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$: for instance
   158	$(q,m,d) = (8,2,1)$ is admissible, while $6 \nmid 8$.  The source performs
   159	the instantiation without addressing the divisibility, so its proof route
   160	establishes the polynomial-pair lemma, and with it the soundness theorem for
   161	the Pauli basis test that rests on it, only for $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.

   163	\section{What the cited soundness theorem requires: the import obligations}
   164	\label{sec:import-obligations}
   165	
   166	The quantum soundness theorem for the classical game inherits the constraint
   167	$m' \mid q$ solely because it is stated for the game just described; its
   168	proof fixes an admissible $q$ with $m' \mid q$, asserts that the game with
   169	simultaneity parameter $1$ is \emph{identical} to the two-prover tensor-code
   170	test for the Reed--Solomon tensor code $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$ of the same
   171	authors' \emph{Quantum soundness of testing tensor codes} (arXiv:2111.08131)
   172	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, and concludes by Theorem~4.7 there, instantiated with
   173	that theorem's auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ in that source,
   174	and written $K$ here to avoid clashing with the field exponent and the
   175	simultaneity parameter --- chosen as $(m')^3 d$.  Neither
   176	the asserted identity nor the instantiation is complete as stated, so the
   177	import carries two verification obligations, which this section details and
   178	which the blueprint's proof node for the soundness statement records as
   179	open.  Both obligations are independent of the divisibility question: they
   180	arise at every dimension, for the $\chi$-based game where it is defined and
   181	equally for the directly indexed variant proposed under the candidate
   182	repairs.
   183	
   184	\paragraph{The cited test.}
   185	In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
   186	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
   187	measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
   188	three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
   189	subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
   190	test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
   191	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
   192	direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
   193	send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
   194	$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
   195	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
   196	last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
   197	in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
   198	one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
   199	the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
   200	test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
   201	pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
   202	answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
   203	test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
   204	$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
   205	--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
   206	distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
   207	$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
   208	consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
   209	lines measurements, and with each other, up to
   210	$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
   211	\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.
   212	
   213	\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
   214	The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
   215	is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
   216	(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
   217	two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
   218	--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
   219	question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
   220	polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
   221	diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
   222	and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
   223	both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
   224	description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of
   225	the pair $(u,v)$, so the constructed measurement must average over the
   226	compatible indices and seeds; and the game's diagonal lines fix the
   227	\emph{first} $i-1$ coordinates where the test's subcubes fix the
   228	\emph{last} $j-1$, so the coordinate conventions must be aligned.  The
   229	construction must preserve projectivity and must match the law of the
   230	hidden-subcube pair with the law induced by the game's diagonal sampling.
   231	(ii)~The game's line questions carry the seed $s \in \F_q$; the test's
   232	carry only the line.  A strategy may depend on the seed beyond its class
   233	$\chi^{-1}(i)$, and removing this dependence runs into the fiber-averaging
   234	difficulty made explicit under the candidate repairs: averaging preserves
   235	the line-versus-point branches exactly but not the synchronicity branches.
   236	(iii)~The branch weights differ: each nontrivial cross-test has mass $1/3$
   237	in the test against $2/9$ in the game.  Once the per-branch predicates are
   238	matched, the intended bookkeeping bound is that the constructed strategy's
   239	rejection probability in the test is at most $\tfrac32$ times the game's
   240	rejection probability, up to the $O(1/(m'q))$ of item~(iv); this bound is
   241	the target of the obligation, not an established fact.
   242	(iv)~The game's predicate fixes an acceptance convention on diagonal
   243	questions with zero direction --- an event of probability at most
   244	$2/(m'q)$, recorded in the blueprint's remark on zero directions --- for
   245	which the test has no counterpart branch.
   246	Finally, the displayed conclusions of Theorem~4.7 pair one prover's points
   247	measurements with the other prover's tensor-codeword measurement, and the
   248	first prover's tensor-codeword measurement with the second prover's lines
   249	measurements, while the game-level statement asserts the point consistency
   250	in both directions; deriving the stated form uses the role symmetrization
   251	of the test and belongs to the correspondence.  None of these steps is
   252	difficult to state, but none is carried out in the source, and together
   253	they replace the asserted one-line identity by a reduction carrying its
   254	own value bound.
   255	
   256	\paragraph{Obligation 2: the parameter bound.}
   257	Theorem~4.7 requires $K \ge 12 m' t = 12 m' (d+1)$.  The source
   258	instantiates $K = (m')^3 d$, which meets the bound iff
   259	$(m')^2 d \ge 12(d+1)$: this holds for all $d \ge 1$ when $m' \ge 5$,
   260	holds at $m' = 4$ exactly when $d \ge 3$, and fails for every $d$ when
   261	$m' \le 3$.  In the game's parameter domain the dimension divides the
   262	admissible field size and is therefore a power of two, so the source's
   263	instantiation violates the hypothesis exactly at $m' \in \{1,2\}$ for
   264	every $d$ and at $m' = 4$ for $d \in \{1,2\}$ --- in particular, in the
   265	multilinear regime $d = 1$, at every dimension $m' \le 4$.  A candidate
   266	repair is to instantiate $K = \max((m')^3 d,\, 12 m'(d+1))$; the open
   267	obligation is then to re-absorb the error, that is, to check that
   268	$\mathrm{poly}(m',t,K)$ and $e^{-K/(m')^2}$ still collapse to the form
   269	$a(dm')^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bm'd})$ in the small-$m'$ cases where the
   270	maximum is $12m'(d+1)$ --- plausible, since there
   271	$e^{-K/(m')^2} = e^{-12(d+1)/m'}$ decays in $d$ at a rate comparable to
   272	$2^{-m'd}$ for $m' \le 4$, but not checked here.
   273	
   274	In the correspondence of Obligation~1, the only role of the divisibility
   275	$m' \mid q$ is to make the $\chi$-sampled index uniform.  The underlying
   276	mathematics does not need the divisibility.  The low
   277	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} samples its axis
   278	index $i$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly, with no index function
   279	on $\F_q$ and no divisibility hypothesis,%
   280	\footnote{See the test figure in \path{references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex}.}
   281	and the tensor-code test is likewise a test about the code
   282	$\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$, not about an encoding of indices into $\F_q$.  The
   283	$\chi$-based packaging exists so that the question distribution is
   284	conditionally linear, which the introspection machinery requires for the
   285	game the players actually play --- the Pauli basis test at dimension $m$,
   286	where admissibility does supply the divisibility.  The game at dimension
   287	$2m+2$ never appears in a verifier; it is an internal analysis device in the
   288	proof of the polynomial-pair lemma, so nothing there requires its question
   289	distribution to be conditionally linear.

   291	\section{Candidate repairs}
   292	
   293	\paragraph{Direct index sampling (candidate direction, recommended).}
   294	Define, for arbitrary $m' \ge 1$, the line-point distribution over
   295	$\F_q^{m'}$ that samples the uniform point, the uniform axis index
   296	$i \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$, and the diagonal direction with vanishing first
   297	$i-1$ coordinates, directly; define the \emph{directly indexed game} with
   298	this question distribution, whose line questions carry the index $i$ (and,
   299	for diagonal lines, the projected direction) in place of the seed
   300	$s \in \F_q$; and state the imported soundness theorem for that game
   301	(form~4 above).  This removes the divisibility obstruction and nothing
   302	else: the directly indexed game still asks for polynomials on revealed
   303	lines, has no pair questions, and weighs its branches as the present game
   304	does, so establishing form~4 carries the same two import obligations as
   305	the $\chi$-based import (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}), now at
   306	arbitrary dimension.
   307	
   308	The relation to the present game when $m' \mid q$ must moreover be proved
   309	at the level of games, not merely of question distributions, because the
   310	two games have different question alphabets: an $\mathsf{ALine}$ question
   311	of the $\chi$-based game is a pair $(u_0, s)$ and a $\mathsf{DLine}$
   312	question a triple $(u_0, s, v')$, so a strategy may select different
   313	measurements for seeds $s \ne s'$ with $\chi(s) = \chi(s')$, and equality
   314	of the induced laws of the geometric data does not by itself transport
   315	such a strategy.  The transport layer decomposes into the following
   316	obligations, none of which is carried out here.
   317	\begin{itemize}
   318	  \item \emph{Distribution lemma.}  When $m' \mid q$, the image of the
   319	  conditionally linear question distribution under the parsing map
   320	  $(u_0,s) \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s))$, $(u_0,s,v') \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s),v')$
   321	  is the direct distribution, and conditioned on the parsed question the
   322	  seed is uniform on the class $\chi^{-1}(i)$, independently of everything
   323	  else.
   324	  \item \emph{Parsing pullback.}  A strategy for the directly indexed game
   325	  composed with the parsing map is a seed-oblivious strategy for the
   326	  $\chi$-based game.  Since the win predicate depends on the question only
   327	  through the parsed data, and a seed-oblivious strategy answers
   328	  identically across each fiber --- in particular on the synchronicity
   329	  branches, where both players hold the same seed --- the value should be
   330	  preserved exactly on every branch, and projectivity is preserved.  This
   331	  is the direction the combining subtree needs.
   332	  \item \emph{Seed-fiber averaging: what it preserves and what it does
   333	  not.}  In the opposite direction, average each line measurement over its
   334	  seed fiber: attach to a direct question $(u_0,i)$, respectively
   335	  $(u_0,i,v')$, the average over uniform $s \in \chi^{-1}(i)$ of the
   336	  measurements attached to $(u_0,s)$, respectively $(u_0,s,v')$, leaving
   337	  the points measurements unchanged.  By the conditional uniformity of the
   338	  seed this preserves the value of every \emph{line-versus-point} branch
   339	  exactly: there the paired question carries no seed, so the branch value
   340	  is an average over the fiber of per-seed values, which the averaged
   341	  measurement computes.  It does \emph{not} preserve the synchronicity
   342	  branches.  There both players hold the same seed, so the $\chi$-based
   343	  branch value is the diagonal average
   344	  $\E_{s}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s)}_f
   345	  \rangle$, while the averaged strategy realizes the double average
   346	  $\E_{s,s'}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s')}_f
   347	  \rangle$ over independent seeds in the fiber; the two differ whenever
   348	  the players' measurements vary across a fiber in a correlated way (if
   349	  both apply a common seed-dependent relabelling, every diagonal term is
   350	  large and the cross terms are not), and neither quantity dominates the
   351	  other in general.  An earlier revision of this note claimed that the
   352	  averaging preserves the exact value, and with it synchronicity; that
   353	  claim was wrong and is withdrawn.  What needs proof is control of the
   354	  synchronicity branches under de-seeding.  Candidate approaches: show
   355	  that a strategy of value $1-\eps$ in the $\chi$-based game is, with
   356	  polynomial loss, close to a seed-oblivious one; or state form~4 with a
   357	  synchronicity hypothesis in the doubled-average form and re-derive it on
   358	  the tensor-code side.  Choosing and proving one of these is an open
   359	  obligation.
   360	  \item \emph{Projectivity round trip.}  The averaged strategy is a POVM
   361	  strategy even when the given one is projective, while the imported
   362	  theorem, like the present one, takes projective strategies.  The
   363	  intended round trip is: dilate the averaged strategy to a projective one
   364	  (Naimark preserves all product correlations
   365	  $\langle X \ot Y \rangle$ of the given strategy against the dilated
   366	  state --- hence the value of every branch the averaging preserved ---
   367	  but nothing restores the diagonal seed correlations once the averaging
   368	  has been performed); apply form~4; and compress the resulting polynomial
   369	  measurement along the dilation isometry back to a POVM in the required
   370	  measurement class on the original space.  That this compression
   371	  preserves the consistency conclusions must itself be proved; it is
   372	  stated here as an obligation, not established.  (Alternatively, form~4
   373	  may be stated for POVM strategies outright, moving the dilation inside
   374	  the import.)
   375	\end{itemize}
   376	
   377	The combining subtree would then be reread with the direct distribution
   378	and the directly indexed game at dimension $2m+2$: every statement becomes
   379	well defined for all admissible tuples, and the expectation is that the
   380	proofs survive unchanged, because the measurements constructed there are
   381	indexed by the geometric data --- points, lines, and polynomials on them
   382	--- and so constitute a strategy for the directly indexed game outright,
   383	with no fiber averaging.  Verifying, lemma by lemma, that those proofs use
   384	only the laws of the sampled objects and never the conditional linearity
   385	of the sampling is part of this direction's obligations.  This follows the
   386	subtree protocol for a definition-level mismatch: the definition is
   387	corrected at the lowest point rather than each downstream lemma acquiring
   388	a hypothesis.  The transport layer costs one parsing-map definition, the
   389	distribution lemma, the pullback lemma, whichever synchronicity control is
   390	chosen, and the dilation--compression lemma; the first three are an
   391	estimated one to two hundred lines on top of the restated import, with the
   392	blueprint's existing Naimark interface supplying the dilation, while the
   393	synchronicity control is the step whose weight is genuinely uncertain.
   394	The external check that the tensor-code test of arXiv:2111.08131 samples
   395	its axes and subcubes directly has been made against that source: Figure~1
   396	there draws the axis index and the subcube data uniformly and directly,

   398	
   399	\paragraph{Padding the dimension.}
   400	Alternatively, embed the combined polynomial into
   401	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,\bar m}(\F_q)$ for $\bar m = 4m$, the least power of two
   402	with $\bar m \ge 2m+2$, ignoring the $2m-2$ dummy variables.  Then
   403	$\bar m \mid q$ holds whenever $q \ge 4m$, and the existing game applies at
   404	dimension $\bar m$.  In the complementary regime $m \in \{q/2,\, q\}$ the
   405	conclusion is vacuous: $md \ge q/2$ gives
   406	$\delta_S \ge a(md)^a q^{-b} \ge a\,2^{-a} q^{a-b} \ge a\,2^{-b} \ge 1$
   407	for $a \ge 2$, while the consistency quantities bounded by the theorem never
   408	exceed $1$.  This route stays inside the present definitions but reworks the
   409	sub-line distribution (a fourth coordinate block of dummies), the combining

   412	
   413	\paragraph{Unequal index classes.}
   414	One could instead define an index function at dimension $2m+2$ with classes
   415	of sizes $\lfloor q/(2m+2)\rfloor$ and $\lceil q/(2m+2)\rceil$.  The index

   417	test fails exactly, and every distributional identity in the sub-line
   418	analysis acquires an error term; this amounts to re-proving the imported
   419	soundness theorem for a perturbed game and is not recommended.

   442	\section{Conclusion}
   443	
   444	There is a theorem-level gap in the source proof route: the classical low
   445	individual degree game invoked at dimension $2m+2$ is undefined for every
   446	admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ (and for $(q,m) = (2,1)$), because its
   447	question distribution requires $2m+2 \mid q$ while admissibility supplies
   448	only $m \mid q$.  The cited route therefore does not establish the
   449	polynomial-pair lemma, nor the soundness of the Pauli basis test that
   450	depends on it, beyond $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.  Independently of the
   451	divisibility, the import of the classical game's quantum soundness carries
   452	the two open verification obligations of
   453	Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}: the asserted identity with the
   454	two-prover tensor-code test must be replaced by a reduction carrying a
   455	value bound, and the source's instantiation of the auxiliary parameter
   456	violates the theorem's lower bound at the small dimensions listed there.
   457	We do not assert that any conclusion is false: the underlying tensor-code
   458	soundness is insensitive to how the axis index is sampled, and both import
   459	obligations concern verification, not counterexample.  For the divisibility
   460	repair, the recommended candidate direction is direct index sampling ---
   461	restate the imported soundness theorem for the directly indexed game at
   462	arbitrary dimension; prove the distribution and parsing-pullback lemmas;
   463	settle the synchronicity control for de-seeding together with the
   464	dilation--compression round trip, so that the present soundness statement
   465	would follow from the repaired import; and reread the combining subtree
   466	against the directly indexed game --- a direction whose open obligations
   467	are enumerated under the candidate repairs, not an established route, with
   468	dimension padding as the fallback confined to the present game definition.

    44	\section{Key theorem forms}
    45	
    46	Three statements must be kept apart.  Throughout, $\game$ denotes a symmetric
    47	two-player one-round game and $\eps \ge 0$ a real parameter; the notation is
    48	introduced in the next section.
    49	
    50	\begin{enumerate}
    51	  \item \textbf{Source form (attainment form).}  If
    52	  $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$, then there exists a symmetric and projective
    53	  strategy $\strategy$ with $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps$.
    54	  \item \textbf{Approximate form (what the source proof establishes).}  If
    55	  $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$, then for every $\eps' > \eps$ there exists a
    56	  symmetric and projective strategy $\strategy$ with
    57	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps'$.
    58	  \item \textbf{Given-strategy form (value-preserving symmetrization).}  If
    59	  $\strategy'$ is any strategy for $\game$ with
    60	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps$, then there exists a symmetric and
    61	  projective strategy $\strategy$ with
    62	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy) = \val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps$.
    63	\end{enumerate}
    64	
    65	The source proof consists exactly of a proof of the third form, applied to a
    66	strategy supplied by the definition of the supremum; this yields the second
    67	form.  The first form asserts strictly more than the second, and the passage
    68	from the second to the first is the gap discussed in this note.  Every use of
    69	the lemma, in the source and in this project, consumes only the second or the
    70	third form.
    71	
    72	\section{The source assertion}
    73	
    74	A two-player one-round game
    75	$\game = (\mathcal X, \mathcal A, \mu, D)$ in compact symmetric notation
    76	consists of a finite question alphabet $\mathcal X$, a finite answer alphabet
    77	$\mathcal A$, a symmetric question distribution $\mu$ on
    78	$\mathcal X \times \mathcal X$, and a decision predicate $D$ treating the two
    79	players symmetrically.  A tensor product strategy
    80	$\strategy = (\ket\psi, A, B)$ consists of a unit vector $\ket\psi$ in a
    81	tensor product $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ of \emph{finite-dimensional}
    82	Hilbert spaces together with POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ for the two
    83	players; its value $\val^*(\game, \strategy)$ is the acceptance probability,
    84	and the value of the game is the supremum
    85	\begin{equation*}
    86	  \val^*(\game) = \sup_{\strategy} \val^*(\game, \strategy)
    87	\end{equation*}
    88	over all tensor product strategies.  A strategy is projective if all its
    89	measurements are projective, and symmetric if the state is
    90	permutation-invariant on $\mathcal H \ot \mathcal H$ and both players use the
    91	same measurements.
    92	
    93	The symmetrization lemma of \cite[Section~5]{Ji2020MIPStar} asserts:%
    94	\footnote{The statement is at
    95	\path{references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex}, lines~94--99,
    96	and its proof at lines~101--132.  The blueprint statement restored to this form
    97	is \path{lem:symmetric-strat} in
    98	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex}.}
    99	if $\game$ is a symmetric game with $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some
   100	$\eps \ge 0$, then
   101	\begin{equation*}
   102	  \exists\, \strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M) \text{ symmetric and projective}
   103	  \quad\text{with}\quad
   104	  \val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps.
   105	  \tag{\path{lem:symmetric-strat}}
   106	\end{equation*}
   107	
   108	Its proof runs as follows.  For every $\eps' > \eps$ the definition of the
   109	supremum supplies a strategy $\strategy' = (\ket{\psi'}, A, B)$ with
   110	$\val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps'$.  By Naimark dilation in the completed
   111	projective form of \cite[Theorem~5.1]{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} one may take
   112	$\ket{\psi'} \in \C^d_{A'} \ot \C^d_{B'}$ for some integer $d$ with all
   113	measurements projective.  One then forms the permutation-invariant state
   114	\begin{equation*}
   115	  \ket{\psi} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}
   116	  \bigl( \ket{0}_A \ket{1}_B \ket{\psi'}_{A'B'}
   117	       + \ket{1}_A \ket{0}_B \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{A'B'} \bigr)
   118	\end{equation*}
   119	on $(\C^2 \ot \C^d) \ot (\C^2 \ot \C^d)$, where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ permutes
   120	the two players' registers, and the block-diagonal projective measurements
   121	$M^x_a = \ket{0}\!\bra{0} \ot A^x_a + \ket{1}\!\bra{1} \ot B^x_a$.  Symmetry
   122	of $D$ gives $\val^*(\game, (\ket\psi, M)) = \val^*(\game, \strategy')$.  The
   123	construction is therefore \emph{value-preserving}: applied to any strategy it
   124	produces a symmetric projective strategy of exactly the same value.  What the
   125	proof establishes is thus the given-strategy form, hence the approximate form;
   126	the printed conclusion is the attainment form.
   127	
   128	\section{Why attainment does not follow}
   129	
   130	The supremum defining $\val^*(\game)$ ranges over strategies on
   131	finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces of unbounded dimension.  The strategies
   132	$\strategy'_{\eps'}$ produced for $\eps' \downarrow \eps$ may require
   133	dimensions $d(\eps')$ growing without bound, and there is no compactness
   134	across dimensions from which a limiting finite-dimensional strategy of value
   135	at least $1-\eps$ could be extracted.  A symmetric projective strategy of
   136	value at least $1-\eps = \val^*(\game)$ would attain the supremum, so the
   137	printed conclusion is equivalent, under its hypothesis, to the assertion that
   138	$\val^*(\game)$ is attained by some strategy.  No general principle supplies
   139	this: it is known, and recalled in the introduction of the source itself, that
   140	the set of finite-dimensional quantum correlations is not closed and differs
   141	from the set of infinite-dimensional spatial correlations, so limits of
   142	finite-dimensional strategies need not be realized by any finite-dimensional
   143	strategy.  Whether some symmetric game realizes the failure --- a game whose
   144	value is attained by no tensor product strategy, presented together with the
   145	exposing functional as a decision predicate --- is a separate question that
   146	this note does not need to settle.  The local verdict is about the proof: the
   147	cited argument proves the approximate form and does not prove the attainment
   148	form.

   150	\section{Uses of the lemma}
   151	
   152	The source invokes the lemma twice.
   153	
   154	First, in the soundness proof for the oracularization transformation, the
   155	argument fixes a strategy $\strategy^{\mathrm{orac}}$ for the oracularized game
   156	``with value $1-\eps$'' and applies the lemma to assume without loss of
   157	generality that it is projective.%
   158	\footnote{\path{references/qpbt-paper/10_oracularization.tex},
   159	lines~317--321.}
   160	Here the input is a given strategy, not the value of the game; the
   161	given-strategy form applies verbatim and preserves the value exactly, so the
   162	use is justified by what the proof establishes.
   163	
   164	Second, in the soundness proof for answer reduction, the argument assumes the
   165	strict inequality $\val^*(\game) > 1-\eps$ and concludes that there is a
   166	symmetric projective strategy of value greater than $1-\eps$.%
   167	\footnote{\path{references/qpbt-paper/11_answer_reduction.tex},
   168	lines~2322--2332.}
   169	Writing $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps_0$ with $\eps_0 < \eps$ and applying the
   170	approximate form with $\eps' = (\eps+\eps_0)/2$ produces a symmetric
   171	projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps' > 1-\eps$.  A strict lower
   172	bound on the supremum thus passes through the approximate form; attainment is
   173	not used.
   174	
   175	In this project, the soundness statements of the Pauli basis test track
   176	quantify over strategies assumed to succeed with probability at least
   177	$1-\eps$, so any symmetrization step starts from a given strategy and consumes
   178	the given-strategy form.  The blueprint currently records the lemma as part of
   179	the games vocabulary and has no downstream dependency on it; the two source
   180	uses above belong to transformations outside the scope of the present
   181	development.  Consequently, no consumer of the lemma --- in the source or here
   182	--- requires the attainment form.

   197	
   198	The verdict is a proof-level gap in the cited lemma: the symmetrization
   199	argument proves the given-strategy and approximate forms, while the printed
   200	conclusion additionally asserts that the supremum defining $\val^*(\game)$ is
   201	attained, which does not follow.  The gap is harmless for the results built on
   202	the lemma, since both uses in the source, and all planned uses in this
   203	project, proceed from a given strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ or from a
   204	strict lower bound on the value, for which the value-preserving construction
   205	suffices.  For stage~4 (formalization) the recommendation is: formalize the

   209	hypotheses or weaken its conclusion silently.  If a later investigation
