We state the quantum soundness of the classical game (Theorem~\\ref{lem:ld-soundness}, imported; see Remark~\\ref{rem:ld-soundness-provider}), the rigidity of the Magic Square game (Theorem~\\ref{thm:ms-rigidity}, imported), completeness of the Pauli basis test (Lemma~\\ref{lem:pauli-completeness}), and the main soundness theorem for the Pauli basis test (Theorem~\\ref{thm:pauli}), whose proof occupies Chapters~\\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}--\\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} and is completed in Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction}. The chapter closes with the qubit form of the soundness statement (Corollary~\\ref{cor:pauli-binary}) and the canonical parameter choice with its soundness bound (Definition~\\ref{def:introparams}, Lemma~\\ref{lem:delta-bound}).\n     7\t\n     8\tThroughout, the two players are denoted $\\mathrm A$ and $\\mathrm B$; for $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$ we write $\\overline w$ for the other player. Games, strategies, values, conditionally linear (CL) functions and distributions, typed distributions sampled from the edges of a graph, and the state-dependent approximation $\\approx_\\delta$ between families of measurement operators are as in Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-games}; the algebraic material on lines, canonical linear maps, the low-degree encoding, and generalized Pauli observables is from Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}.\n     9\t\n    10\t\\section{The classical low individual degree game}\n    11\t% Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.\n    12\t\\label{sec:ld-verifier}\n    13\t\\label{sec:ld-game}\n    14\t\n    15\tThe classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \\in \\F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \\in \\F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\\colon \\F_q^m \\to \\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.\n    16\t\n    17\t\\begin{definition}[The classical low individual degree game: parameters and registers]\\label{def:ld-game}\n    18\t\t\\uses{def:game, def:admissible-size}\n    19\t\tThe game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is parametrized by a tuple $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$, where $m,d,k \\in \\N$, $q \\in \\N$ is an admissible field size (Definition~\\ref{def:admissible-size}), and $m$ divides $q$. We write $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ to emphasize the dependence on the parameter tuple. The type set of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is\n    20\t\t\\[\n    21\t\t\t\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} = \\{\\mathsf{Point}, \\mathsf{ALine}, \\mathsf{DLine}\\}\\;,\n    22\t\t\\]\n    23\t\tand the distribution over type pairs $(t_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B})$ is uniform over $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} \\times \\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$. The ambient space is the direct sum $V = V_X \\oplus V_I \\oplus V_V$ of three register subspaces: the \\emph{point register} $V_X \\cong \\F_q^m$, the \\emph{coordinate register} $V_I \\cong \\F_q$, and the \\emph{direction register} $V_V \\cong \\F_q^m$. Elements of $V$ are identified with triples $(u,s,v) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q \\times \\F_q^m$. The question distribution and the win predicate of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ are specified in Definitions~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} and~\\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} below.\n    24\t\\end{definition}\n    25\t\n    26\t\\begin{definition}[Question distribution of the classical low individual degree game]\\label{def:ld-question-distribution}\n    27\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:cl-func, def:cl-dist, lem:cl-concat, def:cl-canonical, def:line-representative}\n    28\t\tLet $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ be as in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-game}. Define $L_{\\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \\in V$,\n    29\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    30\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-ptf}\n    31\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\\;.\n    32\t\t\\end{equation}\n    33\t\tFor $s \\in \\F_q$, let $\\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that\n    34\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    35\t\t\t\\label{eq:chi-func}\n    36\t\t\ts = (\\chi(s)-1)\\,\\frac{q}{m} + r\n    37\t\t\\end{equation}\n    38\t\tfor some $0 \\le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\\{0,1,\\ldots,q-1\\}$ under the identification of $\\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}. Since $m$ divides $q$, when $s$ is uniformly distributed on $\\F_q$ the index $\\chi(s)$ is uniformly distributed on $\\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$. Define $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ by\n    39\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    40\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-alnf}\n    41\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{ALine}}(u,s,v) = \\bigl(L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u),\\, s,\\, 0\\bigr)\\quad\\text{for all } (u,s,v) \\in V\\;,\n    42\t\t\\end{equation}\n    43\t\twhere $i = \\chi(s)$ and $L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ denotes the canonical linear map with one-dimensional kernel spanned by $v$, used to compute canonical representatives of lines (Definition~\\ref{def:line-representative}). The function $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the concatenation (in the sense of Lemma~\\ref{lem:cl-concat}) of the $1$-level CL function projecting $V_I \\oplus V_V$ onto $V_I$ with the family of $1$-level CL functions $\\{L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}\\}$ on $V_X$ indexed by $i \\in \\{1,\\ldots,m\\}$; thus $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is a $2$-level CL function. Define $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ by\n    44\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    45\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-dlnf}\n    46\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{DLine}}(u,s,v) = \\bigl(L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),\\, s,\\, \\pi_{i-1}(v)\\bigr)\\;,\n    47\t\t\\end{equation}\n    48\t\twhere $i = \\chi(s)$ and $\\pi_{i-1}$ zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input. The function $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the concatenation of (i) the identity on $V_I$, (ii) for each $i$ the $1$-level CL function $v \\mapsto \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ on $V_V$, and (iii) for each pair $(s,v') \\in V_I \\oplus V_V$ the $1$-level CL function $L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{v'}$ on $V_X$; thus $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is a $3$-level CL function.\n    49\t\n    50\t\tThe question distribution of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is the typed CL distribution obtained as follows: sample a type pair $(t_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B})$ uniformly from $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} \\times \\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$, sample $z = (u,s,v)$ uniformly from $V$, and send each player $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$ the question $(t_w, L_{t_w}(z))$.\n    51\t\\end{definition}\n    52\t\n    53\tThe next two lemmas show that the CL functions $L_{\\mathsf{Point}}$, $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$, $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ give rise to the axis-parallel and diagonal line-versus-point distributions.\n    54\t\n    55\t\\begin{lemma}\\label{lem:alnf}\n    56\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\n    57\t\tConsider the pair $(\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\bigl((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0)\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\ell = \\ell(u_0, e_i)$ where $i = \\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\F_q^m$, and $\\ell$ is a line that goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$.\n    58\t\\end{lemma}\n    59\t\\begin{proof}\n    60\t\t\\uses{def:line-representative}\n    61\t\tSince $s$ is uniformly random in $\\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$, the index $i = \\chi(s)$ is uniformly random in $\\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$, so $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\\ell(u_0,e_i)$. Since $u_0 = L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u)$ is the canonical representative of the line through $u$ in direction $e_i$, we have $u \\in \\ell(u_0,e_i)$.\n    62\t\\end{proof}\n    63\t\n    64\t\\begin{lemma}\\label{lem:dlnf}\n    65\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\n    66\t\tConsider the pair $(\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\bigl((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0)\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\ell = \\ell(u_0, v)$ where $i = \\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\F_q^m$, and $\\ell$ is a random diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares its first $i-1$ coordinates with $u$, for uniformly random $i \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$.\n    67\t\\end{lemma}\n    68\t\\begin{proof}\n    69\t\t\\uses{lem:alnf}\n    70\t\tThe proof is identical to that of Lemma~\\ref{lem:alnf}: uniformity of $s$ makes $i = \\chi(s)$ uniform, the direction component of the sampled tuple is $\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ for uniform $v$ (so its first $i-1$ coordinates vanish), and $u_0 = L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u)$ places $u$ on the line $\\ell(u_0,\\pi_{i-1}(v))$.\n    71\t\\end{proof}\n    72\t\n    73\t\\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]\\label{def:line-point-dist}\n    74\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, lem:alnf, lem:dlnf}\n    75\t\tThe \\emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\ell = (u_0,e_i),\\, u)$, where we omit the $0$ components for simplicity. The \\emph{diagonal line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\ell = (u_0,s,v),\\, u)$. The \\emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{Line}}$ is the equal mixture of the two: with probability $\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$, and with probability $\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$.\n    76\t\\end{definition}\n    77\t\n    78\t\\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the classical low individual degree game]\\label{def:ld-win-predicate}\n    79\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:line, def:polyfunc}\n    80\t\tFix $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$. Answers in the game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.\n    81\t\t\\begin{itemize}\n    82\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{Point}$, question content $u \\in \\F_q^m$: the answer is an element of $\\F_q^k$.\n    83\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{ALine}$, question content $(u_0,s) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q$, specifying the axis-parallel line $\\ell(u_0,e_i)$ with $i = \\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple $(f_1,\\ldots,f_k)$ of univariate polynomials $f_j\\colon \\F_q \\to \\F_q$ of degree at most $d$, each given by its $d+1$ coefficients.\n    84\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{DLine}$, question content $(u_0,s,v) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q \\times \\F_q^m$, specifying the diagonal line $\\ell(u_0,v')$ with $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple of univariate polynomials of degree at most $md$.\n    85\t\t\\end{itemize}\n    86\t\tThe win predicate $D^{\\mathrm{ld}} = D^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\\mathrm A}, x_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B}, x_{\\mathrm B}, a_{\\mathrm A}, a_{\\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts.\n    87\t\t\\begin{enumerate}\n    88\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Consistency test}) If $t_{\\mathrm A} = t_{\\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\\mathrm A} = a_{\\mathrm B}$.\n    89\t\t\t% The source phrases both clauses with \"the\" t such that x = u_0 + tv; that phrase\n    90\t\t\t% does not determine t on diagonal questions with direction v' = 0, which the\n    91\t\t\t% question distribution samples with positive probability. The universal\n    92\t\t\t% quantification over t used here is the local correction; see the remark below.\n    93\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Axis-parallel line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\mathsf{ALine}$ and $t_{\\overline w} = \\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,k\\}$ and all $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t e_i$, where $i = \\chi(s)$.\n    94\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Diagonal line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\mathsf{DLine}$ and $t_{\\overline w} = \\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,k\\}$ and all $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$, where $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\chi(s)$.\n    95\t\t\\end{enumerate}\n    96\t\tThe game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the typed game with type set $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$, the question distribution of Definition~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution}, and win predicate $D^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$.\n    97\t\\end{definition}\n    98\t\n    99\t\\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}\n   100\t\tThe source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\\ell(u_0, 0) = \\{u_0\\}$, every $t \\in \\F_q$ satisfies $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \\mapsto u_0 + t \\cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$.\n   101\t\\end{remark}\n   102\t\n   103\tThe soundness properties of the low individual degree game are expressed in terms of the following class of measurements.\n   104\t\n   105\t\\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]\\label{def:ld-meas}\n   106\t\t\\uses{def:polyfunc, def:polymeasurements, def:polynomials-degree}\n   107\t\tLet $\\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ denote the set of POVM measurements indexed by $\\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, the polynomial representatives of individual degree at most $d$ in each variable; this is the notion of Definition~\\ref{def:polymeasurements}, and the argument order $(m,q,d)$ follows that definition (the paper orders the arguments as $(m,d,q)$). By Definition~\\ref{def:polynomials-degree}, evaluation identifies these representatives with the corresponding polynomial functions $g\\colon \\F_q^m \\to \\F_q$, bijectively whenever $d \\le q-1$; the parameter regimes of this chapter (Definition~\\ref{def:introparams} fixes $d = 1$, and admissibility gives $q \\ge 2$) always satisfy this. More generally, for an integer $k$ and tuples $m = (m_1,\\ldots,m_k)$, $q = (q_1,\\ldots,q_k)$, $d = (d_1,\\ldots,d_k)$, let $\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$ denote the set of measurements $G = \\{G_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k}\\}$ such that for each $i \\in \\{1,\\ldots,k\\}$, the outcome index $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i\\colon \\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \\to \\F_{q_i}$ of individual degree at most $d_i$.\n   108\t\\end{definition}\n   109\t\n   110\tQuantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \\emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. Instead, the construction relies on the low \\emph{individual} degree test, whose quantum soundness is proved in~\\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} and generalized in~\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.\n   111\t\n   112\t% The paper states this result in a theorem environment with the label lem:ld-soundness.\n   113\t% We keep both the environment and the label verbatim for cross-reference fidelity.\n   114\t\\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree test]\\label{lem:ld-soundness}\n   115\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:projective-strategy-general, def:tensor-product-value, def:povm-distance, def:bracket}\n   116\t\tThere exists a function\n   117\t\t\\[\n   118\t\t\t\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}(\\eps, q, m, d, k) = a\\,(dmk)^a \\bigl(\\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\\bigr)\n   119\t\t\\]\n   120\t\tfor universal constants $a \\ge 1$ and $0 < b \\le 1$ such that the following holds. For all $\\eps > 0$ and every parameter tuple $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ as in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-game} (so $q$ is an admissible field size and $m$ divides $q$), and for all projective strategies $(\\psi, A, B)$ that succeed with probability at least $1-\\eps$ in the game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$, there exist measurements\n   121\t\t\\[\n   122\t\t\tG^w \\in \\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)\n   123\t\t\\]\n   124\t\ton $\\hilb_w$ for $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$, where by slight abuse of notation $m$, $q$, $d$ denote the constant tuples $(m,\\ldots,m)$, $(q,\\ldots,q)$, $(d,\\ldots,d)$ of length $k$, such that\n   125\t\t\\begin{align*}\n   126\t\t\tA^{\\mathsf{Point},\\, u}_{a_1,\\ldots,a_k} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   127\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   128\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot G^{\\mathrm B}_{[(g_1(u),\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\ldots,a_k)]}\\;,\\\\\n   129\t\t\tG^{\\mathrm A}_{[(g_1(u),\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\ldots,a_k)]} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   130\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   131\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot B^{\\mathsf{Point},\\, u}_{a_1,\\ldots,a_k}\\;,\\\\\n   132\t\t\tG^{\\mathrm A}_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   133\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   134\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot G^{\\mathrm B}_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k}\\;,\n   135\t\t\\end{align*}\n   136\t\twhere $\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}} = \\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}(\\eps,q,m,d,k)$, all three approximations are with respect to the state $\\ket{\\psi}$, and the bracket notation for post-processed outcomes is that of Definition~\\ref{def:bracket}. The first two approximations hold on average over the uniform distribution on $u \\in \\F_q^m$; no question distribution is associated with the third.\n   137\t\\end{theorem}\n   138\t\\begin{proof}\n   139\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:povm-distance}\n   140\t\tLet $\\Sigma = \\F_q$ and let $\\code \\subseteq \\Sigma^q$ be the Reed--Solomon code of degree $d$: the set of all $(p(x_1),\\ldots,p(x_q))$ where $p\\colon \\F_q \\to \\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\\ldots,x_q$ enumerate $\\F_q$. We may assume $d < q$. In the opposite regime the statement is immediate: for $k \\ge 1$ and $d \\ge q$ the prefactor gives $\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}} \\ge a\\,(dmk)^a\\, q^{-b} \\ge q^{a-b} \\ge 1$, while the quantity bounded in Definition~\\ref{def:povm-distance} never exceeds $2$ for families of POVM elements, so the three approximations hold for an arbitrary choice of $G^w \\in \\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$; and for $k = 0$ every answer tuple is empty, all measurements involved are single-outcome, and the approximations hold with error zero. For $d < q$, evaluation is injective on polynomials of degree at most $d$ and a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $d$ vanishes at no more than $d$ of the $q$ points, so $\\code$ is a linear $[q,\\, d+1,\\, q-d]_\\Sigma$ code.\n   141\t\t% The paper prints the parameters as [q, d+1, n-d+1] with an undefined n. With the\n   142\t\t% intended value n = q the printed distance q-d+1 exceeds the true minimum distance\n   143\t\t% q-d of the degree-d evaluation code, and the dimension claim d+1 requires d < q.\n   144\t\t% Both points are corrected above; the regime d >= q, which the parameter tuple of\n   145\t\t% Definition def:ld-game permits, is handled by the triviality argument.\n   146\t\tThe two-prover tensor-code test for the code $\\code^{\\ot m}$, as described in Figures~1 and~2 of~\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, coincides with the game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ with parameters $\\mathsf{ldparams}$ and $k=1$: the axis-parallel line-versus-point test is their axis-parallel lines test, with the roles of the two players chosen uniformly at random, which is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor-code test from Section~4.1 there; the diagonal line-versus-point test is their subcube commutation test, again with the added symmetrization between the players; and the consistency test is their synchronicity test. Theorem~4.7 of~\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, instantiated with its internal parameter $k$ chosen as $m^3 d$ (this parameter is unrelated to the simultaneity parameter $k$ of $\\mathsf{ldparams}$), therefore yields the present statement for $k = 1$. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \\in \\F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \\in \\F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\\colon \\F_q^m \\to \\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.\n    16\t\n    17\t\\begin{definition}[The classical low individual degree game: parameters and registers]\\label{def:ld-game}\n    18\t\t\\uses{def:game, def:admissible-size}\n    19\t\tThe game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is parametrized by a tuple $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$, where $m,d,k \\in \\N$, $q \\in \\N$ is an admissible field size (Definition~\\ref{def:admissible-size}), and $m$ divides $q$. We write $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ to emphasize the dependence on the parameter tuple. The type set of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is\n    20\t\t\\[\n    21\t\t\t\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} = \\{\\mathsf{Point}, \\mathsf{ALine}, \\mathsf{DLine}\\}\\;,\n    22\t\t\\]\n    23\t\tand the distribution over type pairs $(t_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B})$ is uniform over $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} \\times \\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$. The ambient space is the direct sum $V = V_X \\oplus V_I \\oplus V_V$ of three register subspaces: the \\emph{point register} $V_X \\cong \\F_q^m$, the \\emph{coordinate register} $V_I \\cong \\F_q$, and the \\emph{direction register} $V_V \\cong \\F_q^m$. Elements of $V$ are identified with triples $(u,s,v) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q \\times \\F_q^m$. The question distribution and the win predicate of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ are specified in Definitions~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} and~\\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} below.\n    24\t\\end{definition}\n    25\t\n    26\t\\begin{definition}[Question distribution of the classical low individual degree game]\\label{def:ld-question-distribution}\n    27\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:cl-func, def:cl-dist, lem:cl-concat, def:cl-canonical, def:line-representative}\n    28\t\tLet $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ be as in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-game}. Define $L_{\\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \\in V$,\n    29\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    30\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-ptf}\n    31\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\\;.\n    32\t\t\\end{equation}\n    33\t\tFor $s \\in \\F_q$, let $\\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that\n    34\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    35\t\t\t\\label{eq:chi-func}\n    36\t\t\ts = (\\chi(s)-1)\\,\\frac{q}{m} + r\n    37\t\t\\end{equation}\n    38\t\tfor some $0 \\le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\\{0,1,\\ldots,q-1\\}$ under the identification of $\\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}. Since $m$ divides $q$, when $s$ is uniformly distributed on $\\F_q$ the index $\\chi(s)$ is uniformly distributed on $\\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$. Define $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ by\n    39\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    40\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-alnf}\n    41\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{ALine}}(u,s,v) = \\bigl(L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u),\\, s,\\, 0\\bigr)\\quad\\text{for all } (u,s,v) \\in V\\;,\n    42\t\t\\end{equation}\n    43\t\twhere $i = \\chi(s)$ and $L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ denotes the canonical linear map with one-dimensional kernel spanned by $v$, used to compute canonical representatives of lines (Definition~\\ref{def:line-representative}). The function $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the concatenation (in the sense of Lemma~\\ref{lem:cl-concat}) of the $1$-level CL function projecting $V_I \\oplus V_V$ onto $V_I$ with the family of $1$-level CL functions $\\{L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}\\}$ on $V_X$ indexed by $i \\in \\{1,\\ldots,m\\}$; thus $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is a $2$-level CL function. Define $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ by\n    44\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    45\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-dlnf}\n    46\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{DLine}}(u,s,v) = \\bigl(L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),\\, s,\\, \\pi_{i-1}(v)\\bigr)\\;,\n    47\t\t\\end{equation}\n    48\t\twhere $i = \\chi(s)$ and $\\pi_{i-1}$ zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input. The function $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the concatenation of (i) the identity on $V_I$, (ii) for each $i$ the $1$-level CL function $v \\mapsto \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ on $V_V$, and (iii) for each pair $(s,v') \\in V_I \\oplus V_V$ the $1$-level CL function $L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{v'}$ on $V_X$; thus $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is a $3$-level CL function.\n    49\t\n    50\t\tThe question distribution of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is the typed CL distribution obtained as follows: sample a type pair $(t_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B})$ uniformly from $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} \\times \\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$, sample $z = (u,s,v)$ uniformly from $V$, and send each player $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$ the question $(t_w, L_{t_w}(z))$.\n    51\t\\end{definition}\n    52\t\n    53\tThe next two lemmas show that the CL functions $L_{\\mathsf{Point}}$, $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$, $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ give rise to the axis-parallel and diagonal line-versus-point distributions.\n    54\t\n    55\t\\begin{lemma}\\label{lem:alnf}\n    56\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\n    57\t\tConsider the pair $(\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\bigl((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0)\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\ell = \\ell(u_0, e_i)$ where $i = \\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\F_q^m$, and $\\ell$ is a line that goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$.\n    58\t\\end{lemma}\n    59\t\\begin{proof}\n    60\t\t\\uses{def:line-representative}\n    61\t\tSince $s$ is uniformly random in $\\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$, the index $i = \\chi(s)$ is uniformly random in $\\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$, so $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\\ell(u_0,e_i)$. Since $u_0 = L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u)$ is the canonical representative of the line through $u$ in direction $e_i$, we have $u \\in \\ell(u_0,e_i)$.\n    62\t\\end{proof}\n    63\t\n    64\t\\begin{lemma}\\label{lem:dlnf}\n    65\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\n    66\t\tConsider the pair $(\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\bigl((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0)\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\ell = \\ell(u_0, v)$ where $i = \\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\F_q^m$, and $\\ell$ is a random diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares its first $i-1$ coordinates with $u$, for uniformly random $i \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$.\n    67\t\\end{lemma}\n    68\t\\begin{proof}\n    69\t\t\\uses{lem:alnf}\n    70\t\tThe proof is identical to that of Lemma~\\ref{lem:alnf}: uniformity of $s$ makes $i = \\chi(s)$ uniform, the direction component of the sampled tuple is $\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ for uniform $v$ (so its first $i-1$ coordinates vanish), and $u_0 = L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u)$ places $u$ on the line $\\ell(u_0,\\pi_{i-1}(v))$.\n    71\t\\end{proof}\n    72\t\n    73\t\\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]\\label{def:line-point-dist}\n    74\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, lem:alnf, lem:dlnf}\n    75\t\tThe \\emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\ell = (u_0,e_i),\\, u)$, where we omit the $0$ components for simplicity. The \\emph{diagonal line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\ell = (u_0,s,v),\\, u)$. The \\emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{Line}}$ is the equal mixture of the two: with probability $\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$, and with probability $\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$.\n    76\t\\end{definition}\n    77\t\n    78\t\\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the classical low individual degree game]\\label{def:ld-win-predicate}\n    79\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:line, def:polyfunc}\n    80\t\tFix $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$. Answers in the game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.\n    81\t\t\\begin{itemize}\n    82\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{Point}$, question content $u \\in \\F_q^m$: the answer is an element of $\\F_q^k$.\n    83\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{ALine}$, question content $(u_0,s) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q$, specifying the axis-parallel line $\\ell(u_0,e_i)$ with $i = \\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple $(f_1,\\ldots,f_k)$ of univariate polynomials $f_j\\colon \\F_q \\to \\F_q$ of degree at most $d$, each given by its $d+1$ coefficients.\n    84\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{DLine}$, question content $(u_0,s,v) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q \\times \\F_q^m$, specifying the diagonal line $\\ell(u_0,v')$ with $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple of univariate polynomials of degree at most $md$.\n    85\t\t\\end{itemize}\n    86\t\tThe win predicate $D^{\\mathrm{ld}} = D^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\\mathrm A}, x_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B}, x_{\\mathrm B}, a_{\\mathrm A}, a_{\\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts.\n    87\t\t\\begin{enumerate}\n    88\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Consistency test}) If $t_{\\mathrm A} = t_{\\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\\mathrm A} = a_{\\mathrm B}$.\n    89\t\t\t% The source phrases both clauses with \"the\" t such that x = u_0 + tv; that phrase\n    90\t\t\t% does not determine t on diagonal questions with direction v' = 0, which the\n    91\t\t\t% question distribution samples with positive probability. The universal\n    92\t\t\t% quantification over t used here is the local correction; see the remark below.\n    93\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Axis-parallel line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\mathsf{ALine}$ and $t_{\\overline w} = \\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,k\\}$ and all $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t e_i$, where $i = \\chi(s)$.\n    94\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Diagonal line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\mathsf{DLine}$ and $t_{\\overline w} = \\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,k\\}$ and all $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$, where $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\chi(s)$.\n    95\t\t\\end{enumerate}\n    96\t\tThe game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the typed game with type set $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$, the question distribution of Definition~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution}, and win predicate $D^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$.\n    97\t\\end{definition}\n    98\t\n    99\t\\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}\n   100\t\tThe source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\\ell(u_0, 0) = \\{u_0\\}$, every $t \\in \\F_q$ satisfies $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \\mapsto u_0 + t \\cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$.\n   101\t\\end{remark}\n   102\t\n   103\tThe soundness properties of the low individual degree game are expressed in terms of the following class of measurements.\n   104\t\n   105\t\\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]\\label{def:ld-meas}\n   106\t\t\\uses{def:polyfunc, def:polymeasurements, def:polynomials-degree}\n   107\t\tLet $\\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ denote the set of POVM measurements indexed by $\\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, the polynomial representatives of individual degree at most $d$ in each variable; this is the notion of Definition~\\ref{def:polymeasurements}, and the argument order $(m,q,d)$ follows that definition (the paper orders the arguments as $(m,d,q)$). By Definition~\\ref{def:polynomials-degree}, evaluation identifies these representatives with the corresponding polynomial functions $g\\colon \\F_q^m \\to \\F_q$, bijectively whenever $d \\le q-1$; the parameter regimes of this chapter (Definition~\\ref{def:introparams} fixes $d = 1$, and admissibility gives $q \\ge 2$) always satisfy this. More generally, for an integer $k$ and tuples $m = (m_1,\\ldots,m_k)$, $q = (q_1,\\ldots,q_k)$, $d = (d_1,\\ldots,d_k)$, let $\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$ denote the set of measurements $G = \\{G_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k}\\}$ such that for each $i \\in \\{1,\\ldots,k\\}$, the outcome index $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i\\colon \\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \\to \\F_{q_i}$ of individual degree at most $d_i$.\n   108\t\\end{definition}\n   109\t\n   110\tQuantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \\emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. Instead, the construction relies on the low \\emph{individual} degree test, whose quantum soundness is proved in~\\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} and generalized in~\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.\n   111\t\n   112\t% The paper states this result in a theorem environment with the label lem:ld-soundness.\n   113\t% We keep both the environment and the label verbatim for cross-reference fidelity.\n   114\t\\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree test]\\label{lem:ld-soundness}\n   115\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:projective-strategy-general, def:tensor-product-value, def:povm-distance, def:bracket}\n   116\t\tThere exists a function\n   117\t\t\\[\n   118\t\t\t\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}(\\eps, q, m, d, k) = a\\,(dmk)^a \\bigl(\\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\\bigr)\n   119\t\t\\]\n   120\t\tfor universal constants $a \\ge 1$ and $0 < b \\le 1$ such that the following holds. For all $\\eps > 0$ and every parameter tuple $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ as in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-game} (so $q$ is an admissible field size and $m$ divides $q$), and for all projective strategies $(\\psi, A, B)$ that succeed with probability at least $1-\\eps$ in the game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$, there exist measurements\n   121\t\t\\[\n   122\t\t\tG^w \\in \\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)\n   123\t\t\\]\n   124\t\ton $\\hilb_w$ for $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$, where by slight abuse of notation $m$, $q$, $d$ denote the constant tuples $(m,\\ldots,m)$, $(q,\\ldots,q)$, $(d,\\ldots,d)$ of length $k$, such that\n   125\t\t\\begin{align*}\n   126\t\t\tA^{\\mathsf{Point},\\, u}_{a_1,\\ldots,a_k} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   127\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   128\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot G^{\\mathrm B}_{[(g_1(u),\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\ldots,a_k)]}\\;,\\\\\n   129\t\t\tG^{\\mathrm A}_{[(g_1(u),\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\ldots,a_k)]} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   130\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   131\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot B^{\\mathsf{Point},\\, u}_{a_1,\\ldots,a_k}\\;,\\\\\n   132\t\t\tG^{\\mathrm A}_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   133\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   134\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot G^{\\mathrm B}_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k}\\;,\n   135\t\t\\end{align*}\n   136\t\twhere $\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}} = \\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}(\\eps,q,m,d,k)$, all three approximations are with respect to the state $\\ket{\\psi}$, and the bracket notation for post-processed outcomes is that of Definition~\\ref{def:bracket}. The first two approximations hold on average over the uniform distribution on $u \\in \\F_q^m$; no question distribution is associated with the third.\n   137\t\\end{theorem}\n   138\t\\begin{proof}\n   139\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:povm-distance}\n   140\t\tLet $\\Sigma = \\F_q$ and let $\\code \\subseteq \\Sigma^q$ be the Reed--Solomon code of degree $d$: the set of all $(p(x_1),\\ldots,p(x_q))$ where $p\\colon \\F_q \\to \\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\\ldots,x_q$ enumerate $\\F_q$. We may assume $d < q$. 260		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$. 
   261	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}$ be a quantum state, and for all $x\in \mX$,
   262	  $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ two POVMs on $\mH$.
   263	  We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state
   264	    $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   265	  \begin{equation*}
   266	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_a \norm{ (M^x_a - N^x_a) \ket{\psi} }^2 \leq O(\delta)\;,
   267	  \end{equation*}
   268	  and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state
   269	  $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ are clear from context.
   270	  This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance.
   271	\end{definition}

   273	\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]
   274	  \label{def:strategy-distance}
   275	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game
   276	  and let $\strategy = (\psi, A, B)$, $\strategy' = (\psi', A', B')$ be 
   277	  strategies for $\game$.
   278	  For $\delta\in[0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\strategy$ is $\delta$-close to
   279	    $\strategy'$} if the following conditions hold.
   280	  \begin{enumerate}
   281		\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same
   282	    Hilbert space $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
   283		\item For all $x \in \cal{X}, y \in \cal{Y}$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta
   284	    (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations
   285	    holding under the distribution $\mu$, and on either $\ket{\psi}$ or
   286	    $\ket{\psi'}$.
   287	  \end{enumerate}

   314	  \label{fact:add-a-proj}
   315	  Let $\cal{A},\cal{B},\cal{C}$ be finite sets, and let $\mu$ be a distribution
   316	  over question pairs $(x,y)$.
   317	  Let $\{A_{a,b}^x\}$ and $\{B_{a,b}^x\}$ be operators whose outcomes range over the
   318	  product set $\cal{A} \times \cal{B}$.
   319	  Suppose a set of operators $\{C_{a,c}^y\}$, whose outcomes range over the
   320	  product set $\cal{A} \times \cal{C}$, satisfies the condition $\sum_{c}
   321	  (C_{a,c}^y)^\dagger C_{a,c}^y \leq \Id$ for all $a$ and all $y$.
   322	  If $A_{a,b}^x \approx_\delta B_{a,b}^x$ on average over $x$ sampled from the
   323	  corresponding marginal of distribution $\mu$, then $C^y_{a,c} A^x_{a,b}
   324	  \approx_\delta C^y_{a,c} B^x_{a,b}$ on average over $(x,y)$ sampled from $\mu$.

   327	  Fix questions $x,y$ and answers $a \in \cal{A},b \in \cal{B}$. We have then that
   328	  \begin{align}

   330	    & = \sum_{c} \bra{\psi} (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})^\dagger (C^y_{a,c})^\dagger (C^y_{a,c})
   331	      (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b} ) \ket{\psi}\\
   332	    & \leq \bra{\psi} (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})^\dagger
   333	      (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b} ) \ket{\psi} \\
   334	    & = \left \| (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})\ket{\psi} \right \|^2
   335	  \end{align}
   336	  where the inequality follows from the assumption that $\sum_c (C_{a,c}^y)^\dagger
   337	  C_{a,c}^y \leq \Id$.

   341	      \ket{\psi} \right \|^2 	\leq \E_{(x,y) \sim \mu} \sum_{a,b}
   342	    \left \| (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})\ket{\psi} \right \|^2 \leq \delta.

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]

   438	In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
   439		whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
   440	\end{theorem}

   442	\begin{proof}

   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.

   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).

   332		polynomial $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if
   333		$c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when $\alpha_i \le d$ for all $1 \le i \le m$, and
   334		\emph{total degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when

   342		variable, identified by their polynomial representatives rather than by the

     2	"""Check style conventions for changed paper-gap notes.
     3	
     4	This is a local hook guard for ``docs/paper-gaps/*.tex`` notes.  The policy in
     5	``docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex`` is intentionally mathematical rather than merely
     6	syntactic, so this script does not try to certify the content of a note.  It
     7	only catches structural mistakes that reviewers should not have to catch by
     8	hand: missing front sections, missing shared macros and bibliography, and raw
     9	inline traceability which should be expressed through the paper-gap macros.
    10	
    11	The check is diff-scoped by default.  Existing archival notes are not reported
    12	unless they are changed.
    13	"""

    29	    "template.tex",

    31

    36	RAW_LEAN_ID_RE = re.compile(r"(?<!\\leanid\{)MIPStarRE\.[A-Za-z]")
    37	RAW_PAPER_PATH_RE = re.compile(r"(?<!\\path\{)references/(?:ldt|qpbt|neexp)-paper/")
    38	TEXTTT_TRACE_RE = re.compile(r"\\texttt\{(?:MIPStarRE|references/[a-z0-9-]+-paper)")

    49	def _is_note_file(rel_path: str) -> bool:

   154	    if "\\bibliographystyle{alpha}" not in text:

   156	    if "\\bibliography{references}" not in text:

   169	    if RAW_PAPER_PATH_RE.search(text):

   175	def scan_changed_notes(root: Path, changed_files: list[str]) -> list[Finding]:
   176	    """Return findings for changed paper-gap notes."""

## Findings

- [ ] F1 (blocker) `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:135` — `lem:ld-soundness` weakens the source’s consistency conclusions from `\simeq` to `\approx`.
- [ ] F2 (blocker) `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:115` — `def:ld-meas` replaces the source’s function-indexed outcomes with inequivalent polynomial representatives.
- [ ] F3 (changes) `blueprint/src/references.bib:133` — The three new paper-gap entries use repository paths instead of the required published URLs.
- [ ] F4 (changes) `local/protocols/EVOLUTION.md:130` — The ledger records a review-cap amendment and trigger that are absent and unimplemented at this head.

## Review

Changes are required before merge.

**F1.** The source theorem `lem:ld-soundness` uses `\abc[\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}]` at `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:425-433`; `references/qpbt-paper/00_preamble.tex:311` expands that macro to consistency `\simeq_{\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}}`. The blueprint instead states all three conclusions using state-dependent closeness `\approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}}`. This is strictly weaker: `fact:agreement` at `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:227-234` only recovers consistency with the same error when both measurements are projective, while the produced `G^A,G^B` are merely POVMs. In particular, the third conclusion has no converse available. The mismatch is load-bearing because `ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:1195-1200` subsequently consumes self-consistency and point-measurement consistency. Restore `\simeq_{\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}}` in all three conclusions.

**F2.** The source’s `def:ld-meas` at `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:397-407` indexes outcomes by polynomial functions, and its parameter domain at lines 33-35 permits arbitrary positive `d`. The blueprint’s first measurement class instead uses formal representatives and incorrectly claims all chapter regimes satisfy `d \le q-1`. For allowed parameters `(q,m,d,k)=(2,1,2,1)`, `X` and `X²` are distinct representatives but the same function. Separate the source-facing function-indexed measurement class from the project’s representative-indexed Lean class.

**F3.** `docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex:248-252` and `docs/blueprint_style_guide.md:228-236` require blueprint bibliography entries to carry published PDF URLs, reserving repository paths for Lean comments and docstrings. The entries at lines 133, 143, and 153 violate that rule. The comment asserting a local exception does not amend either normative document.

**F4.** `local/protocols/meta.md:32-44` requires the triggering incident, protocol amendment, evolution entry, and affected enforcement changes to be committed together. This head changes only `EVOLUTION.md`: the cited `events.md` incident is absent, `review.md` contains no four-round cap, and the merge tooling does not recognize `review_state: ADJUDICATED`. Remove this unrelated entry or commit the complete amendment and enforcement changes together.

Chapters 11–12 and 14–16 yielded no additional findings. Their remaining symmetrization, combined-lines error, divisibility, and ancilla obligations are explicitly identified as open and are not advertised with `\leanok`. No Lean source changed, `git diff --check` is clean, and local CI was reported green.

VERDICT: CHANGES_REQUESTED
